title: Force–extension graphs and spring constant
keyIdea: When you hang a force on a spring, its extension is how much longer it gets: new length minus original length. Up to the limit of proportionality, extension is directly proportional to force, so F = k e, where F is the force in newtons, e is the extension in metres and k is the spring constant in N/m. A graph of force against extension is then a straight line through the origin, and its gradient is k. A bigger k means a stiffer spring. Past the limit of proportionality the graph curves, and past the elastic limit the spring does not go back to its original length when the force is removed.
familyTip: Hang a bag on a rubber band or a spring and measure how much longer it gets as you add tins one at a time. Measure the stretch from where it started, not the total length.

visual.caption: Which spring constant goes with each spring? Drag each card to a box, or tap it and then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: measure extension not length, plot force against extension, find k from two gradients, load past the limit, and pick the load for 5 cm.

kid: A spring is 10 cm long. You hang 3 N on it and it is now 22 cm long. The extension is how much longer it got: 22 − 10 = 12 cm. Always take away the starting length.

Add the force 1 N at a time and write down each extension. Plot force up the side and extension along the bottom. You get a straight line that starts at zero. Double the force and you double the extension.
This rule is F = k e. F is the force in newtons and e is the extension in metres. The spring constant k is in newtons per metre. It is the gradient of the line. A steeper line means a stiffer spring.
Put e in metres. For a spring with k = 40 N/m, 5 cm is 0.05 m, so F = 40 × 0.05 = 2 N. The rule only works up to a limit. Past it, the line bends. Stretch it too far and it stays longer for good.
adult: Ages 14 to 16. AQA GCSE Physics 4.5.3 (forces and elasticity) states that 'the extension of an elastic object, such as a spring, is directly proportional to the force applied, provided that the limit of proportionality is not exceeded', with F = k e, and it includes a required practical on the relationship between force and extension. Edexcel and OCR cover the same ideas; the work done in stretching (E = ½ k e²) is a separate lesson.

In the lab, students measure extension from a dotted unloaded line, plot six points of a 25 N/m spring, read the gradient of two springs (25 N/m and 50 N/m) with a triangle they drag, load a spring to 10 N to find a limit of proportionality at 6 N, and choose a load for a 5 cm stretch with k = 40 N/m. The curved part and the 2 cm permanent stretch are a simple model, not data for a real spring.

Common mistakes. Students plot total length instead of extension, so the line misses the origin. They keep extension in centimetres and get k a hundred times too small (or F a hundred times too big). Some read the gradient as extension ÷ force, mix up the limit of proportionality with the elastic limit, or think a steeper line means a weaker spring. If the axes are swapped (extension up the side), the gradient is 1/k, so check which way round a graph is drawn.

practice.prompt: A 12 cm spring is 18 cm long with a load. What is the extension?
practice.explain: 18 − 12 = 6 cm. 18 cm is the new length, and 30 cm adds the lengths together.

practice.prompt: A spring has k = {k} N/m. What force (in N) stretches it by 0.1 m?
practice.hint: F = k × e, and the extension is already in metres.

practice.prompt: A force–extension graph (force up the side) goes through (0.05 m, 2 N). What is k?
practice.hint: Gradient = force ÷ extension, with extension in metres.
practice.explain: k = 2 ÷ 0.05 = 40 N/m. 0.025 is extension ÷ force, and 2.5 forgets to change cm to m in the other direction.

practice.prompt: A spring has k = 50 N/m. How many centimetres does a {f} N force stretch it?
practice.hint: e = F ÷ k gives metres. Multiply by 100 for centimetres.

practice.prompt: What happens past the limit of proportionality?
choices: The extension is no longer proportional to the force
practice.hint: Look at the shape of the graph after the limit.
practice.explain: Past the limit the extension grows faster than the force, so the graph curves. F = k e no longer applies.

pool.prompt: Spring X has k = 30 N/m and spring Y has k = 120 N/m. Which is stiffer?
pool.hint: A bigger k means more force is needed for each metre of stretch.
pool.explain: Y needs 120 N for each metre of extension, four times as much as X, so Y is stiffer.

pool.prompt: A force of {f} N stretches a spring by 0.05 m. What is k in N/m?
pool.hint: k = F ÷ e, with e in metres.

pool.prompt: A student plots total length against force. Why does the line not go through the origin?
choices: With no force the spring still has its original length
Force must go on the bottom axis
pool.hint: What is the length when the force is zero?
pool.explain: At zero force the length is the original length, not zero. Plot extension instead and the line starts at the origin.

pool.prompt: A spring has k = 25 N/m. What force stretches it 8 cm?
pool.explain: 8 cm = 0.08 m, so F = 25 × 0.08 = 2 N. 200 N uses 8 instead of 0.08.

pool.prompt: 3 N stretches a spring 6 cm, below the limit. What does 5 N stretch it?
pool.hint: Extension is proportional to force. How many cm per newton?
pool.explain: 6 ÷ 3 = 2 cm per newton, so 5 N gives 10 cm. 8 cm just adds 2 to 6.

pool.prompt: After a big load is removed, a spring stays 1 cm longer than at the start. What has happened?
choices: It went past its elastic limit
pool.hint: Which limit is about going back to the original length?
pool.explain: Past the elastic limit a spring is stretched for good. The limit of proportionality is where the graph stops being straight.

pool.prompt: On a graph with extension up the side and force along the bottom, what is the gradient?
pool.hint: Gradient = rise ÷ run. Which quantity is the rise now?
pool.explain: Rise ÷ run = extension ÷ force = 1/k. With force up the side the gradient is k.

pool.prompt: A spring with k = 40 N/m is stretched by {c} cm. What is the force in N?
pool.hint: Change {c} cm to metres, then use F = k e.
